claims.text: The target material is a quaternary equiatomic FCC solid-solution alloy.
The target alloy has significant local chemical short-range order.
The target alloy has high lattice distortion.
Cryogenic deformation at 77 K maximizes strain hardening.
Cryogenic deformation at 77 K suppresses thermal activation.
Local SRO clusters act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Deformation-induced nanotwins act as barriers to dislocation motion and promote strain hardening.
Under extreme strain, SRO and nanotwin-mediated barriers can trigger a crystalline-to-amorphous transformation.
At low strain rates, yielding is governed by thermally activated dislocation glide over SRO barriers.
Increasing strain rate reduces the time available for thermally activated dislocation motion.
Above a critical strain rate, plasticity transitions from dislocation glide to a deformation-induced phase transformation or amorphization.
At high strain rates, dislocations must overcome barriers by athermal mechanisms or initiate a phase transformation.
The phase transformation absorbs energy and limits further strain hardening.
Yield strength increases with strain rate until a critical rate of approximately greater than 10 s^-1.
Above the critical strain rate, saturation of dislocation mobility by SRO causes the strain-rate sensitivity to fall to near zero.
A stress-strain plateau or softening at high strain rate would indicate phase transformation rather than continued dislocation multiplication.
Pure Ni and Cu continue to strengthen approximately logarithmically with strain rate without undergoing a phase transformation.
The proposed transition applies to equiatomic FCC alloys with high mixing entropy and SRO but may not apply to BCC or non-equiatomic alloys.
The critical strain rate depends on alloy composition and degree of SRO.
Prior evidence associates extreme deformation by high-pressure torsion with structural instability or transformation in CoCrFeMnNi.
